reason: The sources provide enough factual claims to construct a surprising 45-second story about William Lassell and the moon Ariel.
story: In 1851, English brewer William Lassell built his own telescope inside a Liverpool brewery factory and discovered Ariel, one of Uranus's moons. Lassell ground and polished the mirror himself, funding his astronomical passion with the fortune he made from selling beer. Later, astronomer John Herschel named the moon after literary characters from Shakespeare and Alexander Pope. When NASA's Voyager 2 flew past Uranus in 1986, it revealed that Ariel's surface is surprisingly young and heavily grooved by canyons. Scientists now believe that these features were carved by cryovolcanism, powered by ancient tidal heating that may have maintained a subsurface liquid ocean beneath its icy crust.
angle: Uranus's moon Ariel was discovered by a beer brewer using a homemade telescope built inside his factory.

claims.claim: William Lassell discovered Ariel on October 24, 1851.
William Lassell made his fortune as a beer brewer.
John Herschel suggested the names for Uranus's moons in 1852 at Lassell's request.
Ariel is named after characters in Shakespeare's The Tempest and Alexander Pope's The Rape of the Lock.
Voyager 2 performed a flyby of Uranus in January 1986 and imaged about 35% to 40% of Ariel's surface.
Ariel's surface is composed of roughly equal parts of water ice and a dense non-ice rocky component.
Ariel has the most reflective surface of all the moons of Uranus.
No other spacecraft besides Voyager 2 has ever visited the Uranian system.

disputed: Whether John Herschel devised the names of the moons entirely on his own or if Lassell devised them and sought permission; script should attribute the naming request to Lassell and note Herschel suggested them.
